text: But I did come to embrace this new identity. <break time="0.8s" /> And in many ways I think of myself now as African. <break time="0.8s" /> Although I still get quite irritable when Africa is referred to as a country. <break time="0.8s" /> The most recent example being my otherwise wonderful flight from Lagos two days ago, in which there was an announcement on the Virgin flight about the charity work in India, Africa, and other countries. <break time="0.8s" /> So after I had spent some years in the U, S, as an African, I began to understand my roommates response to me. <break time="0.8s" /> If I had not grown up in Nigeria, and if all I knew about Africa was from popular images, I too would think that Africa was a place of beautiful landscapes, beautiful animals, and incomprehensible people fighting senseless wars, dying of poverty and AIDS, unable to speak for themselves, and waiting to be saved, by a kind, white foreigner. <break time="0.8s" /> I would see Africans in the same way that I, as a child, had seen Fides family. <break time="0.8s" /> This single story of Africa ultimately comes, I think, from Western literature. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, here is a quote from the writing of a London merchant called John Lok, who sailed to west Africa in 1561, and kept a fascinating account of his voyage. <break time="0.8s" /> After referring to the black Africans as beasts who have no houses, he writes, They are also people without heads, having their mouth and eyes in their breasts. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, I have laughed every time I have read this. <break time="0.8s" /> And one must admire the imagination of John Lok. <break time="0.8s" /> But what is important about his writing is that it represents the beginning of a tradition of telling African stories in the West. <break time="0.8s" /> A tradition of Sub Saharan Africa as a place of negatives, of difference, of darkness, of people who, in the words of the wonderful poet, Rudyard Kipling, are half devil, half child. <break time="0.8s" /> And so I began to realize that my American roommate must have, throughout her life, seen and heard different versions of this single story, as had a professor, who once told me that my novel was not authentically African. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, I was quite willing to contend that there were a number of things wrong with the novel, that it had failed in a number of places. <break time="0.8s" /> But I had not quite imagined that it had failed at achieving something called African authenticity. <break time="0.8s" /> In fact, I did not know what African authenticity was. <break time="0.8s" /> The professor told me that my characters were too much like him, an educated and middle class man. <break time="0.8s" /> My characters drove cars. <break time="0.8s" /> They were not starving. <break time="0.8s" /> Therefore, they were not authentically African.
